newsitem.title: USA: Reno rejects criticism on campaign finance probe.
newsitem.headline: Reno rejects criticism on campaign finance probe.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno on Thursday rejected charges by Senate Republicans who have accused the Justice Department of hindering their investigation into campaign finance scandals.

At her weekly news conference, Reno defended the Justice Department's decision this week to oppose grants of immunity by the Senate governmental affairs committee to a number of witnesses linked to the scandal.

She said the committee's role of oversight and possible legislation was different from the Justice Department's role to prosecute any criminal wrongdoing in connection with Democratic and Republican campaign financing.

"Our role is to investigate and to prosecute. Not just to prosecute to get a conviction, but prosecute if the evidence is there to get a conviction that will stand up and not be reversed on appeal," she said.
Tennessee Sen. Fred Thompson, the committee's Republican chairman, said Tuesday he had lost confidence in the Justice Department and that it had consistently thrown obstacles into his path.
"I understand his frustration when he talks about delay," Reno said.
She said the Justice Department already has agreed to committee requests for grants of immunity for 11 people, but objected to immunity for nine others.

The committee brushed aside the Justice Department's objections and voted Wednesday to grant immunity to four Buddhist nuns who were allegedly tricked into illegally donating money to the Democratic Party in 1996.

The committee also voted to grant immunity to Keshi Zhan, a $22,000-a-year employee of the welfare department in Arlington, Virginia, who gave $15,000 to the Democratic Party last year. The committee suspects she received the money from Yah Lin Trie, a former Little Rock restaurant owner and friend of President Bill Clinton. Trie has fled the country.
Reno stopped short of saying the grants of immunity would jeopardise the Justice Department's criminal probe. She said the department wanted to be careful not to act prematurely.
"If I immunise somebody, I can hear somebody hollering at me because I immunised somebody and it was the wrong thing to do. You're damned if you do; you're damned if you don't," she said.

The committee is investigating how foreign money was illegally raised and spent in the 1996 elections and whether U.S. security was compromised by individuals who may have shared secret information with foreign business interests.

The Justice Department has been conducting a separate criminal investigation into many of the same allegations and has been concerned that congressional immunity now could make it impossible to prosecute cases later.

Reno also rejected new calls from Republican senators for an independent counsel to take over the criminal probe. "If there comes a point in time where the evidence triggers the independent counsel statute, as I have said, I will do so."
